verses.text: In the month Nisan, in the twentieth year of Artaxerxes the king, when wine was before him, I picked up the wine, and gave it to the king. Now I had not been sad before in his presence.
The king said to me, “Why is your face sad, since you are not sick? This is nothing else but sorrow of heart.” Then I was very much afraid.
I said to the king, “Let the king live forever! Why shouldn’t my face be sad, when the city, the place of my fathers’ tombs, lies waste, and its gates have been consumed with fire?”
Then the king said to me, “What is your request?” So I prayed to the God of heaven.
I said to the king, “If it pleases the king, and if your servant has found favor in your sight, that you would send me to Judah, to the city of my fathers’ tombs, that I may build it.”
The king said to me (the queen was also sitting by him), “How long will your journey be? When will you return?” So it pleased the king to send me, and I set a time for he.
Moreover I said to the king, “If it pleases the king, let letters be given me to the governors beyond the River, that they may let me pass through until I come to Judah;

and a letter to Asaph the keeper of the king’s forest, that he may give me timber to make beams for the gates of the citadel by the temple, for the wall of the city, and for the house that I will occupy.” The king granted my requests, because of the good hand of my God on me.
Then I came to the governors beyond the River, and gave them the king’s letters. Now the king had sent captains of the army and horsemen with me.
When Sanballat the Horonite, and Tobiah the servant, the Ammonite, heard of it, it grieved them exceedingly, because a man had come to seek the welfare of the children of Israel.
So I came to Jerusalem, and was there three days.
I arose in the night, I and a few men with me. I didn’t tell anyone what my God put into my heart to do for Jerusalem. There wasn’t any animal with me, except the animal that I rode on.
I went out by night by the valley gate, even toward the jackal’s well, then to the dung gate, and inspected the walls of Jerusalem, which were broken down, and its gates were consumed with fire.
Then I went on to the spring gate and to the king’s pool, but there was no place for the animal that was under me to pass.
Then went I up in the night by the brook, and inspected the wall; and I turned back, and entered by the valley gate, and so returned.
The rulers didn’t know where I went, or what I did. I had not as yet told it to the Jews, nor to the priests, nor to the nobles, nor to the rulers, nor to the rest who did the work.
Then I said to them, “You see the bad situation that we are in, how Jerusalem lies waste, and its gates are burned with fire. Come, let us build up the wall of Jerusalem, that we won’t be disgraced.”
I told them of the hand of my God which was good on me, as also of the king’s words that he had spoken to me. They said, “Let’s rise up and build.” So they strengthened their hands for the good work.

But when Sanballat the Horonite, Tobiah the Ammontite servant, and Geshem the Arabian, heard it, they ridiculed us, and despised us, and said, “What is this thing that you are doing? Will you rebel against the king?”
Then I answered them, and said to them, “The God of heaven will prosper us. Therefore we, his servants, will arise and build; but you have no portion, nor right, nor memorial, in Jerusalem.”

footnotes.content: Nehemiah served the king's wine—a trusted role, an honored place. Yet his grief over Jerusalem's ruins showed through his face. Even in a position of influence, his heart belonged to what lay broken back home.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The king saw what Nehemiah couldn't hide. One moment of honest sorrow opened a door—fear flooded in, but so did opportunity. Sometimes the Lord uses our visible heartbreak to turn a king's attention toward His work.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jerusalem's gates burned, tombs lay in ruins—Nehemiah spoke the weight of it plainly. His sorrow was legitimate grief for the place where his people belonged and his fathers lay. That honest longing is what moved the king's heart to listen.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A question from the king, and Nehemiah prayed—that quick, hidden prayer changed everything. The Lord hears the silent cry between one moment and the next. That breath of prayer is where real power lies.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Nehemiah asked plainly for what he needed—a real request, spoken with deference but without apology. He knew his place before the king, yet didn't shrink from naming what the Lord had put on his heart.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The queen sat beside the throne, and the king granted his request. Even a servant's faithfulness and honest sorrow can sway the hearts of the powerful—when the Lord goes before us, He opens the way.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: One petition answered, but Nehemiah didn't stop—he asked for letters to the governors. Sometimes the Lord's work requires practical wisdom, not just fervent prayer. He gives us both.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Timber for the gates, materials for the walls—Nehemiah named each need. The king's forest keeper would supply what Jerusalem's workers required. Nehemiah saw how the good hand of God works through earthly means and authority.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The king sent captains and horsemen—a journey with real protection, real resources. Nehemiah didn't go alone or on faith that had no feet. The Lord provides both courage and the practical means to carry it out.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Sanballat and Tobiah heard the news and grieved—evil grieves when good work arrives to challenge it. Their anger was a sign that something true was stirring. The Lord's work often stirs up opposition from those who profit by ruins.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Three days in Jerusalem before moving—time to listen, to let the reality sink in. Sometimes quiet observation comes before bold action. The Lord knows when we're ready.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Nehemiah rose at night with a few trusted companions, his heart full of what God had placed there. He didn't announce his plan—he carried it in secret prayer first. Wise leaders move with God before they move in public.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The valley gate, the jackal's well, the dung gate—Nehemiah rode the perimeter by night, seeing how badly Jerusalem had fallen. The gates were ash, the walls broken. He measured the work ahead with his own eyes.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: At the spring gate, the path grew too narrow for his animal. Destruction had closed off what once was open. Even the land itself reflected the work that lay ahead.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Up the brook, around the broken walls, back through the valley gate—a full survey in darkness. Nehemiah was learning the shape of the work. A leader must know what needs doing before the people join the task.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: No one knew where he went or what he'd seen—not the rulers, not the priests, not the nobles. Some work requires secrecy until the moment is ripe. Nehemiah kept his own counsel and let the Lord guide the timing.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Now Nehemiah gathered them and spoke plainly: 'See the ruin. Rise with me to build.' He named what was broken and invited them to be part of the repair. Great work begins when one faithful voice says, 'Come, let us build.'
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Nehemiah told them of God's good hand and the king's words—both the spiritual truth and the earthly proof. The people saw that the work was blessed and possible. They said, 'Let's rise up and build'—unity found in shared vision.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Sanballat, Tobiah, and Geshem ridiculed the work—mocking is the enemy's first weapon when he sees God's people stirring. They called it rebellion, trying to stop the work before it started. But ridicule is often a sign that something true is threatening what is false.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Nehemiah answered with steady faith: the God of heaven will prosper the work, his servants will arise and build, and the mockers have no part in what belongs to God. Readers today hear an echo of this: when we build what the Lord calls us to build, no opposing voice can claim a share in it. Our portion is His work; theirs is only emptiness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
